Roommate Clause: Keep One Rule
Fourteen house rules. Thirteen crossed out. The last one is about the lease.
Two roommates have broken every house rule but one, right as the lease comes up. Turns out loving someone and signing for her are different decisions.

A year ago, June taped fourteen house rules to the fridge. Riley has crossed out thirteen of them, mostly by being impossible not to like. Now the renewal notice is here, rent is going up, and Riley has already told the landlord yes, with both their names on it. You decide whether Riley can learn to ask before she books, and whether the home and the romance survive being two separate questions.
Their adult friend from the unit downstairs, who helped carry the couch up three flights and has opinions about all of this.
If nobody acts, Riley keeps answering for both of them, and June moves out not because she stopped loving her, but because nobody asked.

One Rule Left
Talk about the renewal notice and the last rule
The kitchen, in front of the fridge
Sunday, 11:40 PM
The fridge list, a year old: FOURTEEN HOUSE RULES, in June's handwriting. Twelve are crossed out in Riley's purple Sharpie.
I cross out number thirteen: Don't borrow my mug. I'm drinking out of her mug right now. It's the best mug.
We have one rule left.
The boring one.
The important one.
I slide the landlord's renewal notice under the magnet, right beneath rule fourteen: Nobody answers the landlord for the other person.
Rent's going up $240. Deadline's the 30th. And she's looking at me like there's a second question under the first one.
What does Riley do?
Talk money now. Get out a calculator.
I pull out my phone calculator and sit on the counter. $2,340 split two ways. $1,170 each. We both stare at it.
Freelance me can do that some months. Not all months. That's the honest answer.
Okay. That's a number. Numbers I can work with.
Riley and June ran the new rent numbers; June said she can afford $1,170 some months, not all.
Ask about the two of you first.
Before the rent. Is this, us, part of the math? Because I don't know how to price it.
I push my glasses up and lose them. It takes me a while to answer.
It's a separate math. I'd like to keep it separate. That's all I can promise tonight.
Riley asked whether their relationship was part of the lease decision; June said she wants to keep them separate.
Say you can't do math after a double.
I did a double. Fourteen hours. If I do math right now I'll agree to anything. Tomorrow, when I have a brain?
Tomorrow. That's a real answer. I'll take it.
I put a sticky note on her mug, my mug: TOMORROW, NOT A MAYBE.
Riley was too exhausted to talk rent after a double; June agreed to tomorrow and left a note on the mug.
Both Our Names
Take back a yes Riley gave in June's name
The kitchen, morning
Monday, 8:15 AM
Coffee's on. June opens her laptop at the kitchen table and finds a CC she didn't expect: Re: Lease Renewal, Unit 3R. Sent 1:52 AM. From Riley.
I read it twice. Hi Mr. Pruitt! We'd love to renew for another year. Riley and June. There's a smiley face.
You signed us up for another year.
I said I wanted to.
You used both our names.
I'm holding a spatula. I put the spatula down, because this is not a spatula conversation.
At 1:52 AM it felt like a love letter. At 8:15 it looks exactly like what it is.
What does Riley do?
Retract it now. CC June.
I type it at the counter while she watches. Correction: I spoke for June without asking. Please disregard. We'll each reply ourselves.
I watch her hit send. Then I draw something on the back of the renewal notice and stick it on the fridge: two stick figures and a question mark.
Tomorrow night I'll have my answer. Not the lease one. The other one. Ask me properly.
Riley emailed the landlord to retract the reply sent in June's name; June left a drawing on the fridge and promised a different answer tomorrow night.
Ask the landlord for another week.
What if I ask Pruitt for an extension? One more week. Nobody's answer counts until we both have one.
And the email that says Riley and June?
I add a line: June hasn't replied yet. Her answer is hers. She reads it over my shoulder and nods.
Tomorrow night. I'll tell you the thing that isn't about rent. Be home.
Riley asked the landlord for a one-week extension and clarified June hadn't answered; June promised to tell her something not about rent tomorrow night.
Keep your yes. Take her name off it.
I'm not un-wanting it. I want to stay, and I'm allowed to say so. But I'll resend it with just my name.
I resend it: Riley would like to renew. June will answer for herself.
I look at her for a long moment, then write on the fridge list, under fourteen: Tomorrow night. Ask me the other question.
Riley kept her own yes but resent it with only her name; June wrote on the fridge asking her to ask 'the other question' tomorrow night.
Room Available
Tell moving out apart from saying no to love
The building's front door
Tuesday, 7:50 PM
June comes home to a flyer on the front door, in Riley's purple Sharpie: ROOM AVAILABLE DEC 1. SUNNY. PLANTS INCLUDED. GREAT ROOMMATE (LEAVING).
I peel it off the glass. Riley is on the stairs with a roll of tape, frozen mid-step, like a raccoon caught in a porch light.
You were mad. I figured you were leaving. I wanted to get ahead of it.
I'm trying to choose you. Stop choosing the ending for me.
I didn't want to get left with the couch.
Or with the feeling?
Both. Obviously both. The couch is just the one I can say out loud.
What does Riley do?
Tear down the flyer. Negotiate the budget.
I take the flyer from her and rip it in half, then in quarters, then into confetti I'll have to sweep up later.
No more getting ahead of it. Kitchen table. Real numbers. You go first or I go first, your call.
I'll get the calculator. You get the good pens.
Riley tore up the sublet flyer and they sat down to negotiate a real budget.
Each look for your own place. Talk love separately.
What if we each look at places on our own, and whatever happens with the apartment, it doesn't decide us?
I fold the flyer and put it in my pocket. Evidence, I tell her.
Yes. Separate searches. And a separate conversation about us that isn't allowed to mention square footage.
Riley and June agreed to search for housing separately and keep their relationship a separate conversation.
Tell Pruitt June's out. Save her the trouble.
I'll just tell Pruitt you're not renewing. You won't have to deal with him at all.
I take her phone out of her hand, gently, and set it on the mailbox.
That's rule fourteen, Riley. Again. From now on, anything with my name on it goes through me. I'll call him myself.
Riley offered to tell the landlord June was leaving; June stopped her and took over all communication in her own name.
Deposit and Feelings
Split the real costs, and don't treat money stress as proof of love
The kitchen table
Wednesday, 10:30 PM
The kitchen table, cleared for once. On the left, June's deposit spreadsheet, printed. On the right, a sticky note in June's handwriting: DATE? That's all it says.
These are two decisions.
I mixed them.
I can like you and need another room.
Like. She said like. I keep my face very normal about it.
Then we price the rooms first.
And nobody signs for both of us.
One name per answer.
What does Riley do?
Price every option tonight. One name each.
We do it line by line: renew here, a cheaper two-bed, two separate studios. Each option gets two columns and two names.
Studios cost more. Together is cheaper. That's math, not a reason to stay.
Agreed. Writing that down so I don't forget it at 2 AM.
Riley and June priced three housing options with separate columns and agreed cheaper-together is math, not a reason.
Take a week. Each finds her own number.
Let's each take a week and figure out our own real number. Alone. No peeking. Then we compare.
No peeking. You're going to peek.
I tape my envelope shut in front of her and write DO NOT on it. She adds PEEK.
Riley and June agreed to spend a week working out their own budgets privately before comparing.
Put the date note away till housing's settled.
I pick up the DATE? note and put it in the drawer with the takeout menus. Not the trash. The drawer.
I'm not letting rent do my asking. When I ask you out, it's going to be on a day that isn't about money.
That's the most romantic thing anyone has ever said to me about a drawer.
Riley put June's date note in a drawer, saying she'd ask on a day not about money; June was touched.
This Sink Is a Crime
Each say out loud what she can really afford
An open house, a two-bed in Point Breeze
Saturday, 11:00 AM
Two bedrooms, $1,850, one radiator that sounds like a haunted accordion. The listing called it charming. The listing lied.
I lean over the kitchen sink. It's avocado green, cracked, and somebody has tried to fix it with what looks like gum.
This sink is a crime.
So was our rent conversation.
I push my glasses up and pull a folded paper from my pocket. It has one number on it. I don't unfold it yet.
No lottery ticket. No rich aunt. Just two people and two real numbers.
What does Riley do?
Say your real number first.
$1,050. Tips swing, so some months $950. That's the real one, not the brave one.
I unfold mine. $900 on a bad month, $1,300 on a good one. We stand over the crime sink and just let the numbers be true.
Okay. Now we actually know something.
Riley said her real budget first ($950–1,050); June shared hers ($900–1,300).
Write numbers down. Swap at the same time.
I write mine on the back of the listing and fold it. On three, we swap. On two, June swaps early.
$1,050. That's more than I thought you had. Why didn't you ever say?
Because I was scared it would sound like I was buying you. Your turn.
They swapped written budgets; Riley admitted she'd hidden hers so it wouldn't sound like buying June's company.
Say you won't take this place. Even cheap.
I can't live with this sink just so we stay together. That's not a budget. That's a hostage situation.
I laugh so hard the agent looks over. Then I nod.
Fair. No crime sinks. Not even for love. Especially not for love.
Riley refused the ugly apartment even though it was cheaper; June agreed they wouldn't compromise just to stay together.
Two Keys, No Contract
Ask for the date before talking about the lease
The living room, on the couch in question
Sunday, 6:20 PM
The couch. Riley's couch, technically. June sits at the other end with her sketchbook and turns it around.
I've drawn two keys. Different shapes. One has a bottle opener. One has a paint chip. There's no contract anywhere on the page.
I want a date before I want a lease.
My whole body goes quiet, which never happens. The radiator fills in for me.
Can we afford tacos?
We budgeted for feelings poorly. Tacos are fine.
She asked me. She asked first. I don't have to plan any of this. I just have to answer.
What does Riley answer?
Say yes. Tacos. Tonight.
Yes. Tacos. Tonight. You pick the place. I'm not planning a single thing, and it's killing me, and I love it.
They go to the truck on Ninth. Nobody mentions rent. June draws Riley on a napkin. It's unflattering and perfect.
Riley said yes to June's date; they got tacos on Ninth Street and never mentioned rent.
Say yes, the day after you both decide.
Yes. But the day after we've both answered Pruitt. I want the date to be the only thing on the table.
I write it on the sketch, under the keys: DATE, THE 31ST. It looks official. It looks like a promise.
Riley accepted the date but set it for the 31st, the day after both answer the landlord.
Say not while you're both moving boxes.
I want to. That's the problem. If we date in the middle of this, I'll start planning your life again. Can we wait until the boxes stop?
I close the sketchbook. Not hard. Just closed.
Okay. I'll keep the drawing. The offer expires never. The tacos might.
Riley asked to wait until the move was over before dating; June kept the drawing and the offer open.
Two Different Keys
Once housing is set, ask again, properly
Riley's phone, during the dinner rush
Three weeks later, Wednesday, 9:40 PM
Three weeks. New arrangements, two different keys: June's has a paint chip, Riley's a bottle opener. Whatever the address, June's door is June's now.
I'm in the walk-in cooler between tables, texting with cold thumbs.
Can I come over Friday?
You used to already be here.
Now I'm asking.
Tacos?
Within the feelings budget.
The taco budget is more reliable.
What does Riley send next?
Make it a real date. Say the word.
Correction: a date. A real one. I'll knock. I'll bring the good salsa. You can still say no.
Yes. A date. Knock twice so I know it's you and not the pizza guy.
I walk out of the cooler grinning so hard a server asks if someone died and left me money.
Riley asked June on a real date for Friday; June said yes and told her to knock twice.
Keep Fridays as friends for now.
Tacos as friends? I like where we are. I want to stay here a while before I ask for more.
Friends with tacos. Best kind. Bring the salsa anyway.
I heart the message, then un-heart it, then heart it again. The walk-in cooler judges me.
Riley and June agreed to Friday tacos as friends for now, taking it slow.
Tell her the truth: you need to stop.
I have to be honest. Every time I see your door, I want to be behind it deciding things. I don't think I should come Friday. Or for a while.
Thank you for telling me instead of vanishing. That was the whole rule, really.
I put the phone in my apron and go back out to the floor. Table six needs more bread. Some things I can fix.
Riley told June she needed to step back from anything romantic; June thanked her for saying it instead of vanishing.
Keep One Rule
Choose: live together, date apart, or end it well
The apartment, the fridge, deadline day
The 30th, 5:00 PM
Deadline day. Pruitt wants answers by six. The fridge list has one rule left standing, and a very old magnet holding it up.
I set two pens on the table. Two envelopes. Two separate reply forms, one name per line.
One name per answer. You taught me that. Kind of by doing the opposite.
I pick up my pen. There are boxes in the hall, some packed and some just pretending. The couch is exactly where it's always been.
Whatever I write, I write only mine. She writes hers. Then we find out what we are.
How does it end?
Renew, both signing. Keep rule fourteen.
I write: Riley Vega, yes. She writes: June Okada, yes. Two lines. Two names. Nobody signs for anybody.
I take the fridge list down, fold away the thirteen dead rules, and tape rule fourteen back up by itself.
Rule fourteen stays. Forever. Now kiss me, that one isn't on the list.
Riley and June each signed their own renewal, started dating, and kept rule fourteen on the fridge.
Live apart. Keep dating.
I write: Riley Vega, not renewing. She writes: June Okada, not renewing. Then June takes out a third sheet of paper.
Separate apartments. Same Fridays. The lease was never the relationship.
Can I come over Friday? I'm asking. I'll keep asking. I like asking now.
Riley and June moved into separate apartments and kept dating, with the lease and the relationship fully apart.
End it kindly. Help her move.
I can't do another round of this. I'm renewing alone. You should go somewhere nobody decides anything for you.
I nod. We split the deposit to the dollar. It's the most careful math we've ever done.
I grab the purple Sharpie and start on her boxes. BOOKS. SCARVES (ALL OF THEM). PENS, DO NOT CRUSH.
I'll label your boxes right.
Riley renewed alone; they split the deposit fairly, ended the romance, and Riley labeled June's boxes for the move.

They did the real math, signed one name per line, and chose the apartment and each other as two separate yeses. Thirteen rules are folded in a drawer. The last one is still on the fridge.
Rule fourteen stays. Forever.

Two apartments, two keys, two leases, and every Friday Riley texts first and waits for the answer. The lease was never the relationship, and now it doesn't have to be.
